speechtext: Order, please. I do not believe that according to the rules the Leader of the Opposition is entitled to make such a statement on motions. subsubtopic: MR. STANFIELD-INCORRECT REFERENCE IN "HANSARD" TO LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION AS AUTHOR OF STATEMENT
speechtext: Order, please. This would require the unanimous consent of the House. The Leader of the Opposition is suggesting a procedure which is entirely unknown to me and entirely new in so far as the rules are concerned. speechtext:
1.	With reference to the News Release dated May 27, 1970, No. 26-70 of the Department of Transport, what steps have been taken to ensure that procedural errors will not reoccur?

November 18, 1970

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerard Duquet (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: DEHAVILAND 125, CF-CFL ACCIDENT
speechtext:
1. The method of handling amendments to Canada Air Pilot in area control centres has been changed to reduce the possibility of error. The methods used, by Unit Chiefs to ensure that these changes are brought to the immediate attention of the Unit Control Staff, have been revised and steps taken to provide a more positive check that all copies of cancelled procedures are promptly removed and destroyed.
2. The "system procedural error", was that the Moncton Centre's copy of Canada Air Pilot was amended by removing the cancelled WK beacon Approach Plate for Wabush Airport, in May 1969. However, there were additional copies of this Plate, contained in Sector binders located at the control boards and through an oversight, these copies were not removed with the result that controllers continued to issue clearances for the "WK" approach after it had been cancelled.

subtopic: CLEARING OF UNDETONATED EXPLOSIVES-MEAFORD RANGE, GREY COUNTY
CLEARING OF UNDETONATED EXPLOSIVES-MEAFORD RANGE, GREY COUNTY
speechtext:
Is it the intention of the government to establish measures for the purpose of collecting any live ammunition that may be hazardous in the target areas of the Meaford Tank Range and, if so, when will this work be done?
Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of National
Defence): Service procedures require that the officer-incharge of live firing exercises destroy any live ammunition that does not detonate on contact with its target. There are, however, instances when such ammunition cannot be located and destroyed. As a general policy, National Defence can not dispose for other uses property that is unsafe. The Defence Research Board is examining feasible technical methods of economically clearing and rendering safe areas polluted with undetonated explosives. This study will include consideration of the particular problem at the Meaford Range. However, it is not known at the present time when this study will be completed, or whether it will be practicable to undertake the task.

Mr. Speaker, during the question period there were several questions which I think arose from a reported statement by Dr. Frank Kelly, a science adviser to the Science Council of Canada to the effect that it is anticipated that about half the Ph.Ds' who will be graduating within the next few months will not be able to
Employment Programs
find work. No doubt this is partly due to inappropriate training in some cases, but surely it also indicates in a very dramatic way the extent of the slowdown in economic development in this country. It also indicates in a very dramatic way the effect this is having even upon highly educated young Canadians.
There can be no question now but that the government has bungled very badly in its economic policies during the past year. Some of us have the impression that the ministers have been so busy admiring themselves they have not really noticed what has been going on in the country. The complacency which has been manifested, particularly in the Speech from the Throne, is in such striking contrast to actual conditions in the country that it is very difficult, when reading the Speech from the Throne now, to believe that it referred to the country in which we have been living these past few months.
The difficulty does not merely arise from the outbreak of terrorism, kidnapping and murder in the province of Quebec; it also arises out of the mounting unemployment that exists in this country. It is true that during this past year or so the government has been busy fighting inflation. This is fine. This is important and it is good, provided it is done with good judgment. But I have the impression sometimes that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) felt he was going to take this country by the neck if necessary and shake inflation right out of it, even if he choked the country in the process.
Because we have been waiting for some relief for the veterans and we have been waiting for some further assistance to older people, we have refused to believe that this country is in such a desperate position that the veterans and older people must pay such a heavy price for the fight against inflation. We wonder what happened to the war against poverty which was declared a couple of years ago. We have wondered why the government has not made some response to the call from the Economic Council of Canada for the Government of Canada to meet headlong the challenge of poverty in this country. What the government chose to do instead was to slow down our economy, the result being the heavy increase in unemployment and an anticipated very heavy increase this winter.
All this, the projected increase in our employment this winter and the projected deplorable conditions that will exist then, has not been taken seriously by this government. One could consider the budget of last spring and the warnings given by all sides of what would happen. May I remind the House that early in August I asked the government to reconvene Parliament promptly for two reasons. One of those was to enable the government to present to Parliament, so that Parliament could discuss them, plans for actively combatting anticipated heavy unemployment this winter. That was last August, but no program has been presented yet.

All this has been brushed aside. The Prime Minister and others have chosen from time to time

N ovember 18, 1970
Employment Programs
to ridicule programs such as winter works. They content themselves with reciting day after day and week after week the few measures that have been taken by the government during recent months, measures which have always proved to be totally inadequate. We had a debate last week, I think it was, on this and related subjects; yet all we obtained from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) was another recital of the things that the government had done. Apparently, there was no recognition at all of the inadequacy of the measures that the government had taken. Now, we have had the Minister of Finance, who has been out west this past week, expressing warnings. The warnings were about the dangers of protection in the United States. We were warned about the danger to Canada arising from certain philosophies held in the United States. I wonder, sir, whether he would not be better off paying a little more attention to the benighted policies of his own government.
I have heard rumours and reports to the effect that officials serving this government are hard at work trying to develop programs at this stage, at this time of year, to fight unemployment this winter. It is reported that this plan will be unveiled soon. I hope so. It is late in the day and the outlook at present is that as a result of the folly of this government the people of this country are going to pay a very heavy price indeed. I hope, sir, that at least one thing will come out of this; I hope that this government will be shaken out of the nineteenth century.
All across Canada unemployment is mounting. We have the unemployment statistics published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics; we have the information that unemployment insurance benefit payments have increased. We had information disclosed in the supplementary estimates considered recently that payments to the provinces for welfare have had to be increased. As a consequence, the supplementary estimates of this government in this area increased by $51 million. This, in part, is the result of increased unemployment. Of course, an incidental effect of it will be that very heavy burdens will be laid upon the municipalities and provincial governments involved. It is bad across the whole country, sir, and it is particularly bad in slow growth areas. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand, Langelier) is not present. But I say to the minister, through you, sir, that the economic slowdown in this country and the pronounced effect that will have on our slow growth areas is such as to virtually make a mockery of the efforts of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion in his attempt to encourage development in those areas.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) pointed out in the question period how little had been done for his province, at any rate, by that department. Yet even where the effort of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion has been substantial, even where the effort of his department has been substantial, that effort could accomplish nothing in view of the slowdown and the demoralizing effect resulting from general economic policies prevalent in this country as well as the discouragement that results from the slowdown in the national rate of growth.
All this, sir, is particularly hard on such areas as Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, but the effect is not confined to them. Actually, differing rates of unemployment in various areas are themselves one of the best indicators of how serious this problem has become. British Columbia, the Atlantic provinces and Quebec are all going to suffer a great deal this winter. Of that there can be no doubt. The amount of aid available through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is not going to help very much, and the extra money that the government has promised is pretty ridiculous when contrasted with the need. This is another example of this government's lack of concern, and of its lack of effective policies, in doing anything of importance to smooth out these dangerous discrepancies.

speechtext:
I do not want to be altogether unfair about this. In its own way, the government has done something along this line. It is true that the areas of high unemployment are still there, and that the unemployment is getting higher. But there has been one development in that the areas of relatively low unemployment are becoming scarcer and scarcer, and they may even soon vanish altogether. The Prairies are expecting a rate double that of last year and Ontario appears to be heading for its greatest number of jobless in a good many years. That, sir, is equalization according to the style of the present government. If you cannot cure poverty, spread it around. I wonder what it is going to do for an encore.
What does unemployment mean in concrete terms, sir? Even to the person and community still relatively untouched by unemployment, it has a real, though subtle, significance. It means lost opportunities for the businessmen; it means a lower standard of living for the family and for the community; it means at the very least a certain sense of insecurity. Actually, it means everything that comes from living in an economy that is working at far under its own potential, in an economy that is therefore insecure. This is the effect of mass unemployment, even on those who do not seem immediately to be affected, or directly affected. It is different for those who perhaps are not yet personally affected and who live in a city or town where unemployment is rife. The feeling of insecurity is much more pronounced; social morale is down; business and commerce of all sorts are much more directly hit. The community itself is poor; it cannot afford to spend money even for social essentials. It tends to become run-down.
It should not be necessary to talk about the people, the wage earners and the families who are directly involved. But with this government, it seems to be necessary time after time to remind it what this means in terms of loss of human dignity, of vanishing hopes and of a bitterness towards society. This loss of human potential and of human resources may well be more than temporary, because a man can be out of work for so long that he loses a great deal of his drive, and even his sense of personal dignity. A prolonged period of joblessness for a

November 18, 1970

proud man can be a terrible thing. It can destroy his willingness and even his ability to work. That is one of the dangers of the prolonged and massive type of unemployment that this country has been experiencing. And it will go on experiencing this more intensively according to the forecasts. No government should need to be reminded of this, but it seems that this government must be reminded.
I will not take time this afternoon to speak about social unrest. Certainly, I am not going to suggest that political terrorism and support for political terrorism are a direct result of mass unemployment. That would be far too simple an explanation and it would not be right in any event. Yet, surely it is obvious even to this government that unemployment of this type creates a social climate where whole groups of men are embittered to the point where they begin to think about violent attempts at solutions, even if they are not yet accepted.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Along with human poverty, loss of individual dignity and social unrest, there are of course the economic effects of unemployment. I should not have to remind a government that has put so much stress on economic statistics that mass unemployment means a lowered input into that system, combined with a higher level of unproductive demand on that same system. As the Economic Council of Canada points out in its latest report, when an economy is working below its potential, there is no way of it ever recovering the losses that it sustains during such a period. That is an absolutely irrecoverable loss.
And yet this government does not seem to be unduly concerned. The Minister of Finance is quoted as having said yesterday that everything is looking up-that prosperity is just around the corner, so to speak. Well, I hope it is pretty sharp corner because, if it is not, the promise does not mean very much. In fact, on the face of it, it looks simply like a new expression of the complacency we have come to expect from this government. It tells more about the government than it does about the economy of this country.
It seems a long time ago, in terms of the events that have taken place, but it was just a little more than a month ago that the government produced what still has to be considered as the utmost example of complacency, the Speech from the Throne. We were described as a country somehow calmer and better than the others, despite our tiny little problems that the government was going to solve for us. We were even on the verge of greatness. I would say rather than the government was on the verge of lateness. The government's tardiness in all fields, from security to economic management, has been amply demonstrated ever since. I say that with no joy. All hon. members in this House are Canadians and have no desire to see this country in trouble. But neither can we deny the existence of the signs that we are in some trouble. That is why I am sorry I have to remind the government about the effects of its policies. We must keep insisting until we get action. It should not be necessary, as I said before but, unfortunately, in view of the
Employment Programs
apparent lack of concern that this government has demonstrated, we in the opposition must do so.
This government, and let us make no mistake about it, has responsibilities that it cannot simply slough off. It is very easy to blame business, it is very easy to blame labour unions, farmers, or any other groups you might care to mention, for the economic problems we are facing. The government has not been shy about blaming other people. And when it runs short of people it will even blame humanity in general. It is greed that is to blame, as the Prime Minister said last September when he was discussing unemployment in a speech in Quebec.
If the Prime Minister wants to blame human frailties, I suggest he choose a few others. How about incompetence on the part of the government? How about a lack of concern on the part of that same government as to what is happening to the workers and to the economy of this country? What about complacency? There is the real ally of the devil. And it is a quality that this government has in abundance.

One of these days we will have to discuss trade policy because that is another area of complacency. We are talking about matters of more immediate concern. I hope that this government does not repeat the steps it has taken because the steps that have been taken have been inadequate. I hope no one will do what the Prime Minister did some time ago with regard to housing, rise and say that there is no crisis. The housing situation is serious, as is the unemployment situation. It is late in the day to attack the problems of this winter, but we must try.
I have made these suggestions before. First, the government should have an immediate conference with the piovinces, move forward on projects and discuss other methods of stimulating employment this winter. All the municipalities and provinces have projects on which they can move forward, if they can solve some of their budgetary problems. This conference should examine the position of some of the municipalities and provinces with regard to their capacity to meet the responsibilities they will have to discharge this winter in terms of welfare.
Second, the government should review the position announced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) about a week ago that no interim changes were planned with regard to the amount and duration of the unemployment insurance benefits or the qualifications required to earn these benefits. This would be useful and should be studied.
Third, the Minister of Finance should present an immediate budget which, among other things, should indicate a clear direction to the economy, not a continuation of the ambiguous statements being made by the minister such as "We will encourage the economy to expand as rapidly and as soon as we think it is efficient for it to expand". What does that mean? In what way does that indicate to the business community or the country the concrete way in which the government

N ovember 18, 1970
Employment Programs
would like the economy to expand? To what extent does this indicate in a tangible way the economic goals of the government for the immediate future? To what extent does it give guidance to the business community or the community as a whole as to the basis of its plans.
The government should concentrate on tax reductions.
It should remove the sales tax on building materials used in the construction of housing. This would provide an immediate stimulus throughout the country in terms of employment as well as providing additional homes for Canadians. A reduction in income tax should be more than an elimination of the surcharge that was added to fight inflation. This would not be inflationary. It would be interesting to see whether such a move would reduce the inflationary pressures resulting from rising wages. It would not necessarily affect government revenues because the expanding economy would produce additional revenues. Perhaps just as important as far as the private sector is concerned, the government should remove as quickly as possible the uncertainty with regard to the unpegged dollar and our exchange rates, as well as the main outlines and positions on tax reform which are causing the uncertainty. The government should immediately indicate its position with regard to the modifications in the white paper proposals as suggested by the House of Commons and Senate Committees.
There are other suggestions that can be considered. I say to the government, through Your Honour, let us get going. During the past two years inequalities have increased in this country. That is unfortunate, but it is true. Inequalities have increased as between regions and among individuals with regard to opportunity. There has been increased poverty among the aged and the unemployed. I say people are paying a heavy price for the complacency of this government and I sincerely request that the government give us today not merely a recital of what has been inadequately done in recent months, but what it proposes to do. Unless the government comes forward today or tomorrow with some concrete proposals reassuring us of its energy, its concern and its effectiveness, I certainly call upon this House to support this motion.

speechtext:
I was pleased to note that during some part of his speech today the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) addressed himself to the words of the motion. I must say I thought he was probably in a mood to repeat once again a speech which he has made before in the hope that its impact would grow with retelling. Unfortunately, it does not seem to be having that effect, although I must say that when he refers to the difficult situation of individuals who are unemployed, of individuals who find themselves in difficult circumstances, his speech is improving, probably because he has been using the eloquent words spoken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on this aspect of the subject.

The Leader of the Opposition seems to find difficulty in appreciating what is involved in solving the inflation problem while at the same time producing an atmosphere in which the economy, and employment opportunities, can expand. It is true the Leader of the Opposition did note that there was inflation to be fought, and that this was an important task, but he did not seem to realize the natural economic impact of attempts to get the economy under control. It appears to me that members opposite fail to appreciate the tremendous importance to this country of the private sector and of decisions made in that sector of the economy; the government's monetary and fiscal measures can, it is true, have an important effect-but only an effect-on those decisions.
The economy of this country is basically sound and is capable of moving forward along a path which now seems to lie clearly ahead. It was vital, though, that inflation be brought under control-vital for the sake of those on relatively fixed incomes, vital for the sake of every region of this country. We have begun to succeed in this task. When we began, we made it clear that in our view the controlling of inflation, so fundamental to long term growth, could have a serious impact upon immediate employment levels unless marked restraint were exercised by all sectors of the economy in their claims as to the amount they would like to take out of the economy in return for their services. We urged restraint upon business, upon labour and upon all groups in this country to the end that more people might be employed in the production of goods at lower cost. This is simple economic truth which I should apologize for repeating were it not so clear that members opposite do not understand it.
Our dilemma at this time arises from the need to maintain a firm hand on inflation within the economy. The Leader of the Opposition talked about additional expenditures and tax reductions without showing any concern for their effect in terms of inflation. I should not say he showed no concern; his words were "It would be interesting to see the effect-." Well, it is not hard to foretell the effect of removing all constraints on economic policy. Surely, the road to an expanding economy, to growing employment, is to build and maintain confidence within the whole of the economy and particularly within the private sector, in its readiness and ability to grow and move forward. It is inflation itself which has been, in its way, a deadly throttler of growth in the private sector. It is confidence in the economy which will, in itself, bring about more investment. What are needed at this point are firm decisions on the part of the private sector in the economy to move forward.
The Leader of the Opposition asked for a signal. Surely, that signal has already been given in terms of announcements which demonstrate the determination of the government to deal with inflation and create a climate in which jobs can be provided through investment and growth. There remains a serious issue in relation to the amounts sought to be taken out of the economy by those who are strong and, at the same time, unwilling to moderate their claims. I know from what they are saying that members of the Tory party would not like to see restraints applied to the business community. And I know
November 18, 1970

we shall hear from our friends in the New Democratic Party how wrong it would be if the restraints of good sense were applied to certain other sectors of the economy. It is important they be applied to all.

This government has been concerned not only about those regions having special economic difficulties but also about those groups of people who have special problems. In addition, it has been concerned about the fact that as long as inflation is allowed to continue it will be these people who will suffer the most. It is our determination, as it is our responsibility, to see that the economy is put into such sound shape that inflation is under control; that an atmosphere is created for additional employment opportunities, particularly in the private sector of the economy; that the private sector is able to move forward and, together with the public sector, take steps to create the employment that is required.
We on this side of the House have faith and confidence in the economy. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion presented by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) criticizes the government because its opposition to full employment has increased economic inequalities in this country. It also criticizes the government because its refusal to introduce short-term and long-term programs has resulted in recession-level poverty and social injustice in this country. It seems to me that the facts that are apparent in Canada today fully bear out these grounds for condemnation.
The government's decision to precipitate an economic recession in order to combat inflation has caused injury to the entire society of Canada. However, it has fallen with undue severity upon the depressed areas and segments of our society. When the government decided to curb inflation by precipitating an economic recession, it took no steps whatever to safeguard those areas of Canada which were already adversely affected by economic conditions.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) has stated that the government is valiantly trying to combat inflation but that it cannot put any programs to work without reviving that inflation. He went on to say that the members of the New Democratic Party were opposed to any limitation being placed on the incomes of those in certain sectors of the economy. The minister is either not paying any attention to what is going on in the House or he is playing fast and loose with the facts. The members of this party have repeatedly said, and moved motions to the effect, that we believe the government should long ago have imposed a prices and incomes policy.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The only two stipulations we made were that an incomes policy should cover all forms of income, not just wages and salaries but also prices, profits, interest rates and rents, and secondly that it should not freeze those who are on very low incomes but should allow them to be raised to a reasonable level. That is the position we have taken. When the Minister of Manpower and Immigration says they want to curb inflation and stop it, then I ask why on earth do they not get on with the job. No one is stopping them imposing a mandatory prices and incomes policy. If they asked the provinces they would receive the co-operation of most of them. They, of course, have been victims of inflation.
There is no doubt that the government's policy has not only affected employment all over Canada generally but has caused more unemployment in those areas which already had less employment, particularly the province of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. Now the Prairie provinces, which generally do not have unemployment, have seen a very sharp rise in unemployment.
Not only are regions affected by the government's policy but also segments of society itself, those least able to protect their own interests such as farmers, fishermen, small businessmen and those in the service industries. These have suffered because when the government started its policy of fiscal and monetary restraint it did nothing to make sure the areas already adversely affected were not subjected to still further depression. This government has forsaken the basic goals set by the federal government and the governments of all the provinces at the end of the Second World War. When the war was over, we started out to build a new Canada and all governments agreed there were two goals toward which we should move. The first was full employment with a high level of income. The second was the right of every Canadian no matter where he or she may live to enjoy a high standard of health, education and welfare services. I point out, although it is unnecessary to do so, that the government certainly has failed in respect of this first objective. The government has not managed to obtain full employment. This is shown by the latest figures issued by the government.
The unemployment figure for October is shown as 419,000. That does not include those persons receiving training, farm labourers, or the women and a number of other people who drop out of the labour market through sheer frustration. The total would probably represent half a million people. But the figure of 419,000 is 105,000 higher than the total for the previous year. The most unfortunate part of the statistics is that 188,000 of the unemployed are young people 24 years of age and under. This afternoon the minister boasted about the large sums of money the government is paying for training. We in this party support these expenditures for training. For years we advocated the setting up of a manpower training department. Certainly, we will continue to support such a vote and give the minister all the co-operation we can. But that is only part of the program. If you train people you must have jobs when their training is completed. At the rate we are spending money on training without any programs to provide jobs, we will have the most highly trained unemployed force in the world and we will develop a race of perpetual students and perpetual trainees.
The fact is that we now have pockets of poverty all across Canada. The situation is worse in some provinces than in others. The Economic Council of Canada says that between 4 million and 5 million people live on or below the poverty line and that more than 3 million people live in a state of deprivation. In other words, 7 million or 8 million Canadians are unable to enjoy the full employment and high level of income we started out to establish 25 years ago. The tragedy, however, is that this poverty is concentrated mainly in certain areas of Canada and particularly in the poorer provinces. The government in the course of this debate probably will tell us that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is solving this problem. Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that the effectiveness of the government's program to reduce regional disparity is not measured by the amount

November 18, 1970

of grants given to large corporations. It is measured by the results.
On November 16 this year, in an answer to a question asked by my colleague the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton), we find that by the use of the Regional Development Incentives Act some $95.5 million has provided 17,284 jobs. That I believe is an average of some $5,500 of capital investment per job. But let us look at the unemployment picture issued by the Economic Council of Canada. In Table 3 of their report we find that in 1970 the increase in the number of persons employed is
77.000.	That is the lowest increase since 1958 when we actually had a deficit. The tragic thing is that of those
77.000	persons employed, about two-thirds were in the province of Ontario. In the Atlantic provinces, the increase is only 1,000. In the Prairies there is an increase of 1,000. In the province of Quebec there is an increase of
3.000	and in the province of Ontario an increase of
49.000.	Measured by those statistics, the government's program for removing regional disparity is a colossal failure.
This afternoon when speaking on behalf of the government the minister commented on the concern which has been expressed by both the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance. No one is complaining about the lack of expressions of concern. But what we are complaining about is the lack of action and the lack of concrete programs and specific policies that will help get the economy going, put the unemployed to work and remove the pockets of poverty that obtain all across this country. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration said it is up to the private sector to make the decisions about investment. Now, we have another scapegoat. Some time ago it was labour because it would not agree to freezing wages and salaries while interest rates and profits went sky high. Now, the scapegoat is to be the private sector which is not prepared to make the necessary investment decisions.
Let us look at the Department of Regional and Economic Expansion. We find that the large part of the expenditures which they have made, about two thirds of them, consist of grants which were paid to United States corporations. In the period to the end of 1969 they have paid to foreign corporations $46,176,000, and to Canadian firms only $20,877,000. Some of these companies received these grants from the government by closing a plant, for instance, in Oshawa and opening another one in Hawkesbury as did Duplate of Canada, which is hardly likely to help reduce regional disparity.
[DOT] (4:20p.m.)
If we are going to deal with the problem of regional disparity, it seems to me we have to do something more than make grants to manufacturing firms. We have to deal with community involvement. We have to deal with industries that are indigenous to the community. We have to be prepared not to wait, as the minister says the government is doing, for the private sector to make investment decisions. We should be prepared to work through Crown corporations federally and provincially.
Employment Programs
We should be prepared to help support co-operatives, farmers and fishermen's co-operatives, for the processing of their own products. We should be prepared to support community feeder lots, sawmill operations, tourism, food processing, and not rely entirely on persuading large corporations to come into a community where, in many cases, their sole purpose is to pay low wages and have very little relationship with the community itself.
I think the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has failed to state clearly what its objectives are and what its criteria are. I have in my hand the third report and review of the Canadian Council on Rural Development which was submitted to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) in July of this year. I do not have the time to quote from it extensively, but I am sure that every member who has read it will realize that it is a very trenchant criticism of the way that department is being operated. Page 63 of the report reads:
In the first place, a development programme of any kind needs to identify with reasonable precision its goals and objectives. Secondly, programmes must be instituted consistent with these goals and objectives. These programs must be continuously evaluated both in terms of their effectiveness and in terms of priorities.
The next page reads:
There is no evidence that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has, thus far, established this kind of objective basis for its programmes. There is a possibility that the department may come to measure its own success in terms of how many grants it has provided to industries, how many factories have located in designated areas, how many jobs have been created, and so forth. This can lead to maintaining programmes that should not be continued, or only in revised form, but also to termination of reduction of programmes without adequate rationale. The undoubted uncertainty and confusion about the value and effectiveness of the ARDA programme over its years of existence can be traced in very significant degree to this lack of precise definition of targets and objectives in the context of a plan.
It seems quite apparent that if the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is to be effective, it must be increasingly concerned about the infrastructure of the communities in order that the whole milieu of the depressed area can be assisted by the department and by an infusion of public funds. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration said today that the government is waiting for the private sector to make investment decisions. But when it makes those investment decisions, there is no guarantee that those decisions will benefit the depressed areas of this country. I wonder if the government has given any thought to the program which the Swedish government introduced many years ago, called the capital investment reserves program. It seems to me that this is something at which the government ought to look. Under that program in Sweden any company can take up to 45 per cent of its undistributed profits and deposit them with the bank of Sweden, draw interest on that money, withdraw the money any time it likes, but must pay income corporation tax on it. But if a company is prepared to draw that money at a time when the economy is slack and to invest it in areas where the government requires development, then it can withdraw
November 18, 1970

Employment Programs
those capital investment reserves without paying the tax on the money which it has deposited. During the time that I, along with a group of economists, spent a month studying this and other policies in Sweden, I was tremendously impressed with the fact that they have been able to move industries into more depressed areas and to control the location of industries. The result has been that they have been able to maintain a very high degree of employment and of economic activity.
I want to go on to another question but since I see that my time is almost up may I read the amendment that I propose to move? If the House will let me spend just a few minutes on it, I would like to do so.
I move:
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and this House condemns the government for aggravating these conditions by its policy of opting out of its responsibility to be involved in the maintenance of national standards in health, welfare and education.
I began by saying that 25 years ago the governments federally and provincially had set two goals: full employment and a high level of income and national standards of health, welfare and education. I am contending in this amendment that the goverment has aggravated the situation by continuously opting out of many of the programs which were designed to maintain national standards.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad that this motion makes it possible for us to clearly assess the situation, to analyze the government action and to bring in constructive suggestions. It is not because special circumstances seem to give the government a comforting cover that we should forget the situation which exists now in our country.
The gross disparities alluded to in the motion under consideration are so obvious that we wonder whether we live in such a large and rich country where life is so enjoyable. In fact, the disparities between the privileged classes of society and the various categories of workers, of pensioners, in short the disparities between French Canadians and English Canadians, are inconceivable.
Mr. Speaker, a quick analysis of this situation, shows us that there is no concentration of effort to reach an agreement between the propertied classes and the workers to make everyone feel really good and ready to contribute to the best of this ability, to the progress and the development of our people.
November 18, 1970

How can such flagrant income disparities be explained? Some citizens receive an annual income of $6,000, $7,000, $8,000, $10,000 or even $20,000 while others live on salaries of $1,200 and $1,500. How can such a situation exist? The figures are here to prove that it does and they are bewildering. Union activities have succeeded in obtaining reasonable wages in most trades. However, there is still a great number of workers who would rather forfeit their starvation wages and go to the nearest social welfare office to pick up the slim allowance cheque. When one has lost taste for work and effort, we can only fear the unforseeable and disastrous consequences of such decadence.
It is therefore in order to wonder, with regard to the present situation, what the government has done to check such decadence. We can clearly see that the government has not done anything and that the situation still prevails.
The inequality between the large and the small family is, in my view, the most flagrant injustice. We have reached the point where we accept the fact that "large family" means poverty and "small family" means affluence and wealth. And yet, the worthiest, the noblest and the most important contribution of Canadians to their nation is the one they make through their blood: their children.
When considering the millions of dollars we pour into immigration, one wonders where the logic is. Family allowances are still at a ridiculously low level although several opposition members, particularly from the Rallie-ment creditiste, have repeatedly asked that something be done about it.
Such disparity, such inequity which affects the very core of a nation, namely the family, seems to me most revolting.
Publicity is used to lure immigrants to this country. I have nothing against immigrants, but I wish we would start exercising sound and well-ordained charity to provide our citizens who do not have to adjust to our country, because they were born here with at least the possibility of bringing up their children properly and turning them into assets for the common good.
Inequality is found also in welfare measures, including unemployment insurance. A white paper on unemployment insurance was tabled and we hope that the problem can be solved once for all.
Somewhat foolish rules result in officials telling the unemployed: Unfortunately, you have no more stamps; it is over, go back home, you can receive no more payments. And yet that person must continue to live and to provide for his dependents, if any. What has been done in this connection? A white paper has been issued. We shall wait for the concrete results of this policy.
As for inequality between Canadians, depending on their ethnic origin, it is useless to insist on this subject. An inquiry on bilingualism and biculturalism has given fantastic statistics on this subject which could explain several embarrassing situations which now plague Canada.
Employment Programs
It is inadmissible that salaries should vary depending on the ethnic origin of the employee and yet this situation which exists in Quebec, in the Montreal area, is defended by a number of Liberal members who seem unaware of what is going on before their eyes and who are always ready to criticize those really willing to contribute to the economic growth, to the welfare and to the emancipation of all Canadians whatever their ethnic origin.
In connection with this situation, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government are boasting about the extraordinary fight they have been waging against inflation.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
We still do not know exactly what this fight consisted of, even though we heard about it many many times. This quixotic fight which they claimed to have won, brought no concrete changes in the life of the Canadian people. Why wage a fight which gives no results? And only the arrogance of the government and of the Prime Minister seem satisfied. For the people the same situation prevails, when it is not a defeat.
The action of the government boils down to pious wishes which, in theory, seem to be attainable ideals. The just society, we await it, we have awaited it, and we will continue to await it. We are ready to co-operate closely in order to achieve it, but until now, it has simply seemed to be very pious wishes and nebulous theories, and we do not know exactly where this is going to lead us.
The action of the government has also consisted in answering by a definite no to the provinces which were trying to solve, through tax reforms or others, the special problems of each region. And, as a matter of fact, the motion blames the government for not doing that.
The action of the government only went as far as to tell the provinces, "Go back home, and if you need more money, collect more taxes. We do what we have to do; you do the same". In theory, this looked like a solution to the problem, but we know that when it comes to putting into practice the principles of federalism, wich they would like to be well alive and quite co-operative, and which they adorn with all kinds of adjectives, they give flat noes as answers to the provinces.
There is also the systematic and intentional increase in unemployment. This is the worst scheme, the most disastrous action, and they are beginning to boast about it. They boast that they are solving the problem of inflation by intentionally increasing the number of unemployed. That beats all, Mr. Speaker, and nevertheless the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has every chance, every opportunity to take more popular measures which would solve the real problems.
Some action was taken by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which, admittedly, was rather effective in certain cases. There is still, however, something mysterious in the designation of special zones, and one wonders why they bother to say that a community or
1300

Employment Programs
area is designated as a special zone, when problems are known to affect all regions and all areas. This may be only window-dressing at times, but it seems that a certain effort has been made in this connection.
We now come to our suggestions, because it is not enough to criticize and to establish facts; we must act. As usual, our suggestions are clear, precise, concrete, even though we are accused of bringing forward vague solutions. They keep saying that without ever taking the trouble to specify what is vague about those solutions.
Making available to citizens money and real credit, corresponding to the real guarantees the country possesses, there lies the open secret, something very simple, and we come back to the suggestions implicit in the principle that it is money that should serve the citizen and not the citizen who should serve money.
Mr. Speaker, let us take as a starting point what the Prime Minister himself advocated in 1954, and not the statements emanating from the leader of the NDP. As the leader of the Ralliement creditiste (Mr. Caouette) said this week, let us take as a starting point a statement made in 1954 by the Prime Minister, as follows: "Happily, there is a remedy that can be applied instantly, at the first sign of weakness in the national economy: it is to stimulate purchases by putting more money into the hands of the consumers."
It may seem unbelievable, but our present Prime Minister said that in 1954.
Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to fully agree with that statement which had already been made by another one of his predecessors, Mackenzie King. All we want is that this be done. Let there be a declaration of war on inflation, but let the choice of weapons be the right one.
To go moose hunting, one does not use a slingshot or a peashooter. Therefore, in order to really fight inflation, the best weapon should be to increase the purchasing power to increase consumption and, consequently, give an invigorating shot-in-the-arm to all producing businesses. That is still what we suggest.
It is possible to ease the burden of provinces and municipalities by giving them access to the Bank of Canada.
Will they finally answer that question? Why do the premiers of Quebec and of other provinces have to go and ask permission of New York bankers to build a dam, a bridge or a school? On account of what principle do we cringe to that extent? Is it because we have no guarantee? Have we not enough resources in our country to guarantee the actual credit that we want and advocate? We should put an end to that stupid procedure under which we have to ask foreigners permission to do something here.
It is not because they have never been implemented that our suggestions are wrong! That is the kind of argument we always hear: Money does not grow on trees; if that solution were adequate, it would have been applied elsewhere. We must apply it for the first time. Before the caveman saw a wheel for the first time he had
to imagine one and build it. It is not because other people did not think of that solution that one should not apply it.
When a policy to abolish inequalities will be considered, when a concrete policy will be suggested to provide everyone with the strict minimum, when we become convinced that our country has everything to provide everyone with this strict minimum, we will have found the solution.
To conclude, we urge the government to implement some if not all of the basic principles which we have been advocating for many years. I said it before in this House, we have no exclusive rights on the monetary reform we advocate. The government is quite free to draw inspiration from it. We will support it in its task. We must stop thinking about the advisability of doing one thing or another and listen to those who advocate it.
The pretense that our party represents only a few constituencies does not justify saying that what we are advocating is not good. We must stop living in the clouds and identifying the whole government with one man who pretends to be in the limelight and finds nothing better to do than to cover his head with feathers and play drums to draw the attention of the people of this country. It is time to end such childishness and to tackle the basic problems. We have to mix with people, know their opinions, their problems, their aspirations. We must listen to the people and muster everything in order to give to all Canadian citizens the possibility of looking forward to better days.

Mr. Speaker, in this country we are faced today with a very formidable taks, that of providing 500,000 additional jobs by this winter and in the future to keep unemployment at an acceptable level of around 3 per cent of the work force. Today my leader, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), very ably outlined the steps which the government must take to stimulate the economy and make it possible for additional industrial activity to provide additional jobs for our people. Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal, in the few minutes which are available to me this afternoon, with one particular aspect of the problem facing us, and that is the difficult task of providing the jobs which we need in the underdeveloped areas of this country where unemployment is considerably higher than in the other parts of the country.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the best way to increase employment in such areas is to work out a means by which we can attract more manufacturing industry, which is, of course, by far the greatest employer of labour, to those areas. That, of course, raises the question, can this be done? The answer is yes. The other question, "Well then, how can that be brought about", I intend to deal with now.
It has been obvious for many years that we have been shipping overseas a far too large proportion of the raw materials which we produce, for people in other countries

November 18, 1970

to process into finished products, which mean for them the great benefits of employment and profits which accrue from manufacturing. This loses for us, in Canada, those benefits which I believe can and should be ours.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that we in this country possess all the ingredients which are necessary to make this country into one of the really great industrial nations of the world. We have the raw materials, the cheap power, the transportation, and the skilled manpower. We have a certain amount of capital of our own, and we have proved that we can attract additional capital from the outside world without too much difficulty. What we need is far more manufacturing industry in this country to transform a far greater proportion of the raw materials which we produce into finished products.
How can we bring this about? I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it can be done by means of an industrial development incentives plan which would offer such generous incentives to companies which have proved their ability to manufacture successfully, both in Canada and in other parts of the world, that they will decide it is to their financial advantage to establish plants in areas which the federal government would designate, areas which need industry to balance their economies and make them less dependant on their production of primary products.
Despite the introduction of the government's regional development program, persistent unemployment of around 10 per cent in the Atlantic provinces, in Quebec and in British Columbia shows very clearly that, with the exception of the larger cities in those areas, there has been far too little development of manufacturing industry which, as I said, is by far the greatest producer of employment. It is obvious that the incentive which the government has offered has not appeared to be sufficiently rewarding to attract the number of new industries which we need to keep employment at a satisfactory level in those areas, and that an additional incentive is required. I have no quarrel with the government's plan. It simply is not enough, and that has been proven by the unemployment figures prevalent in our country today. The plan I am going to suggest would act in addition to the government's plan, and would not interfere with it in any way.
In working out such an additional incentive, we must remember that unless what we offer is sufficiently attractive to persuade companies that it is well worth their while to establish plants in those areas where we need them, they will simply decide not to establish plants in such areas. The taxes and the employment which would have been available to those localities will simply not materialize.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I believe that the kind of incentive which industries need to persuade them to operate in areas not normally considered to be economically attractive must convince those industries that two things will happen. First, they will be able to make a satisfactory profit. Second, they will be able to obtain the additional capital they need at a cost which they can afford to pay. I will deal with each in turn.
Employment Programs
The kind of incentive which I believe will convince industry that the first condition will be met, is freedom from paying taxes, federal, provincial and municipal, for the first ten years of operation, and a graduated scale of taxation for the next 15 years. After 25 years of operation, they will pay full taxes. As a large proportion of taxes are provincial and municipal, concurrence of the province and, through them the municipalities, will be necessary to make the policy work. However, these taxes are not now being paid, because the industries in question do not exist and will not exist unless they are persuaded that it is worth while for them to establish in these slow growth areas. I am sure that the prospective construction, employment and future taxes will persuade the provinces and municipalities that the plan makes possible such attractive prospects for the future they will agree to participate in it. Any province or municipality which does not wish to enter the plan would, of course, be free to stay out.
To enable municipal governments to finance the cost of services which would have to be installed to enable these new plants to operate, the federal government should make available loans at no more than 5 per cent interest and payable in 25 years. Although this would impose a cost of 5 per cent on the municipalities, I am convinced that the construction; additional sales by merchants in the district; the employment which would provide taxes to the municipalities instead of having to pay welfare; additional house-building, and a great many other benefits which would accrue to the locality, would more than compensate the locality concerned for the payment of the 5 per cent interest on the cost of producing the necessary services.
The second requirement, that of being able to obtain the capital that industry needs at a rale that it can afford to pay, would be met by investment in the enterprise by the Canada Development Corporation when it comes into existence, which I hope will be soon. I believe that participation by the CDC as a minority shareholder in any of these enterprises which need additional capital would be an excellent kind of investment for the Corporation to make. I stress minority position because it is essential that the government should not get into the business of running industries, and should rely on the management skills of already proven enterprises to successfully direct the new plants which would come into existence through the introduction of the development incentive.
I am convinced that the plan I have outlined will be sufficiently attractive to persuade many successful producers, both in Canada and in other parts of the world, that it will be worth while for them to establish additional plants in this country, close to sources of raw materials. I have discussed this plan with a great many industrialists that I know and with whom I have had dealings in the past, both as a minister of the government and in private business. They have told me that they believe a plan of this kind would be extremely attractive and practical, and that it would persuade many industries in Canada and outside the country to establish in areas which would be designated by the government.

Because taxes from which the new developing companies will be freed for the first 25 years are not being paid now, nor will they be paid unless the companies concerned find the government's offer sufficiently attractive to persuade them to establish additional operations in these slow growth areas, the plan will not impose any cost on the governments concerned, nor on the taxpayers of Canada.
I believe that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) should now call a federal-provincial conference, which should include representatives of the provincial mayors and reeves associations, to discuss the details of a development incentive which will be sufficiently attractive to persuade the manufacturing industry to establish plants in areas which badly need industry to balance their basically primary product economics, and overcome seriously rising unemployment. When the policy has been agreed upon, it should be put into practice at the earliest possible moment.

Mr. Speaker, I feel the present government has been generous in its legislation providing incentives for industry. But we have to realize that no government can solve all the problems of the under-developed rural sections of Canada. This task must be undertaken in co-operation with the business community and with the assistance of labour.
There seems to be a feeling on the part of some of our labour unions that they are not permitted to undertake and develop new enterprises. I would urge not only the
[Mr. Hees.l

business world but the labour unions to join the rest of Canada and the various governments at federal and provincial levels in helping to develop the rural parts of this country. This is not a task which should be left to any particular government or to any particular segment of society; the co-operation of all segments is needed. I believe that if some of the money which union organizations presently remit to the United States were retained in Canada and used here as a starter for equity capital to establish new industries, a great deal of employment could be created.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion has been providing a large proportion of the dollars spent on setting up the services required before new industry can establish itself in under-developed areas. The department has spent a great deal of money on hydroelectric power installations, roads, water supplies, sewage installations and other services required by a normal, operating community. There is no basis whatever for opposition statements that nothing has been done in this connection. I question very much whether more industry would be attracted, even if more generous grants were made. If the government becomes more generous, the tendency is to say: this is government money and it need not be spent with any degree of efficiency. I could give some examples to the House by way of illustration. An outstanding example is the heavy water plant in Nova Scotia. Here is a plant which cost several hundred millions of dollars, for which funds were made available. The design and engineering were inadequate as the basis for a properly operating plant, and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was eventually called upon to advance further financial help. A large additional amount was then spent on redesigning and reconstructing the project. The plant is now successful, but the cost per job turned out to be in the order of $8,000 or $9,000, far above the average amount required to provide employment in the rural parts of Canada.
Opposition speakers have suggested that new industries locating in under-developed areas should not be required to pay taxes of any kind for a period of ten years. But who will be called upon to pay the additional cost of the auxiliary services such as roads, water, sewers, power lines, schools and so on which go to make up a viable economic and social unit? These are the services normally provided by municipal governments, and they are extremely costly. To say that the money will be advanced by the federal government at 5 per cent means that somebody in our social structure will be called upon to pay higher taxes. I, for one, feel that taxes today are already far too high.
There is a tendency on the part of certain members of our society to speak too glibly and too freely of welfare. It is encumbent on every Canadian to encourage his fellow men to be independent, to find their own way and to resort to welfare only when it is really needed. I know that many hon. members have personal experience of instances when welfare funds have been abused; out of every dollar spent, less than 50 cents finds its way into the hands of those who really need help. In my view, Mr. Employment Programs
Speaker, the initiative shown by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has led to one of the finest and best types of incentive program we have ever seen in Canada. If the opposition feel they can improve on it, fine and dandy.

This afternoon I listened very attentively to the argument supporting the contention that we should be more generous with our incentives. I am not convinced. I am not convinced because I, too, am associated with others in my constituency who have shown some initiative in creating new industry. These are people who have had to pioneer new industry in the same way as our forefathers built this country. This is the type of person we need to develop the business world in Canada and to create new industry.
We have the people and we have the motivation. I think it is now a question of a little more education. At the present time our incentive program is conducive to establishing new industry. For example, where else could any member of this House today set up a new industry and be given a 50 per cent grant? Suppose I was prepared to invest $1 in a certain industry, having worked out my rate of return spread over 7, 10 or 12 years, the federal government through its Department of Regional Economic Expansion would be prepared to give me a grant of up to 50 per cent of my cost, with no strings attached except that I must stay in business for three years. If I have no intention of staying in business for more than three years, then I should not start any kind of business.
The financial incentives presently offered by the government are good ones. However, I think there is one thing we have lacked. I should like to ask every member of this House, to how many of his constituents has he explained the incentive program in a proper and precise way. I wonder how many members have even seen the application form issued by the department. A high percentage of applicants in my area have been successful in getting grants, thus creating a substantial number of new jobs. Every new job creates revenue in the form of deductions for personal income tax, sales tax, municipal tax and insurance costs. In addition to that there is added cash flow in the community. All of these factors build a broader base for the economy and contribute more tax dollars to the coffers of the provincial and federal governments.
During the last day or so there has come across the desks of all hon. members a booklet entitled "Financing Canadian Industries," prepared by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. May I again congratulate the department for taking the time to analyse in crystal clear fashion just what is involved in the financing of Canadian industries. The booklet explains what is equity, what is risk capital, what is loan capital. It also outlines some of the provincial agencies, all of which are anxious and willing to support anybody who is prepared to start an industry but able to put up only 50 cents on the

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in this debate during which will be discussed most particularly the possibility of checking poverty and of removing by the same token a social injustice now widespread in Canada. It was quite normal to discuss this matter in the present context, in view of the difficulties we are facing now.
It is clear that every responsible government has the duty to create a climate of confidence. Certainly, it is difficult to create such a climate when we know that about 30 per cent of the Canadian people now live in poverty. In the last few years, insecurity has become prevalent here in Canada as well as the deterioration of the social environment.
As far as young people are concerned, they refuse to identify themselves with society. How could they agree to it blindly? In fact they have lost confidence not only in Parliament but also in its individual members.
The difficulties we are facing now may be due to the rapid evolution we have undergone in the past few years. It seems that youth craves liberty very much. To my mind, it is not only by dictatorial legislation that we will succeed in establishing a new atmosphere of confidence. The mere passage of legislation will not endow our society with a better way of life than the one we are enjoying at the present time.
I believe that it is the responsibility of the government to adopt the measures likely to fulfil the aspirations of Quebecers and all other Canadians.

It might be advisable to convene, as soon as possible, a summit meeting made up of representatives of the federal and provincial governments and of labour and management associations. Such a meeting would enable responsible members to discuss our present problems. In my view, such a meeting is necessary because it would represent not only the interests of governments but also those of the Canadian community. In fact, it would be beneficial to everyone.
Has the government really tried to give, for instance, to the young people, that freedom they are craving for, and which is the product of an evolution experienced throughout the world and not only in Quebec or in other regions of Canada? Has the government done its utmost to enable them to find summer employment?
I know that we spend millions, and I would even say that this is wasted money in some cases, to allow a certain number of young people to find summer jobs. Some people have suggested the establishment of compulsory military service, thought I do not feel that through such a dictatorial law we could solve this problem or satisfy youth.
I have always considered that the majority of our young people are full of good faith and prepared to build a better Canada. I have thought that a disciplinary training service, with pay, would perhaps be required, or at least valuable. We could in this set up mix business with pleasure, as people often say, allow all young Canadians, over the summer period, to join voluntarily this training service which would give them a certain discipline and would train men for peaceful purposes instead of training soldiers to wage war.
But who would be responsible for that disciplinary service? Would it be the federal government or the provinces? I would be inclined to think that the federal government should make some funds available to the provinces anxious to make use of such a service, ensuring to those young people an income which would enable them to continue their studies while giving them the opportunity of attaining manliness, as we all wish.
Such a service should be voluntary, because we have to take into account businessmen and farmers who need their children during the summer to work at home. But a responsible government could, through such an initiative, enable each province to take advantage of such a service and would allow thousands of young people to earn an income sufficient to improve their education and also practice the elementary discipline to which we must all submit in this world.
Since this would be a voluntary service, it would allow young people to reach university level with an excellent record. Application of this program would not involve a much greater cost to the taxpayer, since the young people, having earned an adequate income during the summer, would not need to apply to provincial governments for scholarships.
This program would give us an opportunity really to assess our young people and to know exactly how many of them want, not merely training, but work, and the experience of earning a dollar and investing it in themselves and the community as a whole.
November 18, 1970

This formula could help to improve the difficult situation we are now witnessing. Unemployment and poverty co-exist and there is talk of checking poverty.
In the name of inflation, thousands of unemployed have unfortunately been created, unemployed who still cost the government, directly or indirectly, about $100 a week. I have always thought that a citizen who works regularly is of far greater advantage to the government.
I find it hard to understand exactly to what extent, in the name of inflation, our economy can be stabilized again while the expense is being allowed of up to $100 a week per unemployed who could otherwise still work and be worth something to Canada.
Yet, the winter works programs were allowed to go by the board without hesitation. I had thought that, under the circumstances, supplementary credits would be granted hurriedly to provinces and municipalities in order to allow them to carry out priority projects and this at special rates. It is unthinkable that we continue to tolerate borrowing at exaggerated rates. I venture to believe that the government is as aware of these possibilities as we are. Indeed, the purpose of this debate is not necessarily to criticize the government, but to allow each member to contribute in finding a solution-however small-liable to reestablish the stability of society.
All members are aware of the reduced credits allocated to various departments and Agriculture was not spared. It was sad to let some producers fall into unemployment by cutting subsidies for agricultural production, which did not leave them any other recourse than social welfare. Suggestions were made by opposition members. I had the pleasure of saying a few words on the question, Mr. Speaker, but we did not win.
I hope that knowing what conditions prevailed last spring, the government will do something. As lately as yesterday, I did not agree to a reduction of some subsidies. On the contrary, producers forced to abandon agriculture for serious motives should be given an alternative. I think the responsible government was under the obligation of creating jobs, giving retraining programs and offering advance pensions. Finally, this has often been mentioned before a subsidy reduction was considered.
We hope the government will change its mind and favour that position, particularly with regard to the working class.
As I am dealing with social injustice, in the next few minutes, I would like to talk about amendments to the constitution. The subject may not seem related to the matter now at issue, but it has a connection with the social climate we have to create.
Our constitution must be changed because it is outdated, no doubt about that. In fact, a number of Canadians, both in and outside Quebec, cannot accept the idea that federalism in its present form can provide well-being in Canada. I
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that young people in particular will no longer be satisfied, as they have been up
Employment Programs
to now, with unacceptable compromises. More than ever, I think that the members of this House will have to be very honest with our youth.
As a consequence of the government's hesitation in introducing certain changes, we are now facing the problems of poverty and social injustice. And these problems make the members of this House vulnerable in the eyes of both the young and the rest of the Canadian people.
We have the responsibility to create an atmosphere of confidence for all. It is surely a great challenge to take up, but it is needed. By being more administrators than politicians, we will succeed together in creating this climate of confidence. We will succeed if we apply ourselves to the protection of our industries by adopting certain measures which would give them some necessary incentives.
No doubt the measures applied by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion are necessary and beneficial, but I think that we have forgotten our industries too long. We have also forgotten to consider the new importance of short-term pump priming in the building trade. Once again, I urge the government to consider seriously removing the 12 per cent tax on building materials and the possibility of paying back some interests to those who have a low or an average income.
My time is running out fast, Mr. Speaker, and I would still have many things to say. I dare hope that these few comments will help the government to eradicate this poverty and social injustice which afflict not only the people of Quebec, but of all Canada.
