I am very pleased that a vote will be taken on the motion introduced by the opposition so that the wish of the House can be expressed on this important matter. We have been very concerned in the last few weeks, particularly those of us who are not as emotionally involved as are others in what has been happening, that some of the problems facing Canada arise not from differences but from the same problems that occur in a number of regional areas in Canada. The fact that for a number of years now regional programs have been in effect to assist in the improvement of parts of Canada on a regional basis, programs which have not achieved their goals, has tempted some hon. members I am sure to take a look at some of the solutions offered by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) in his very interesting speech this afternoon.
Some of the proposals of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings have been tried out in many countries. Recently, I saw an advertisement for the Bahamas which announced a ten year tax free period for industry locating in that area. The fact is that in many of these countries this tax free period has benefited the development of industry with the result that the area has been faced with the same problems which we had recently in Jamaica. Canadian investment was encouraged in that

November 18, 1970
Employment Programs
country, and then questions were asked as to whether or not the industry was used to the advantage of the depressed area or solely to the advantage of those who benefited from it in the first place.
Before that type of incentive is applied to the depressed areas in Canada, we should consider some of the major problems that are affecting us, one of them being our Canadian sovereignty in terms of industrial development. I come from an area where incentives have been applied for the last five or six years. Hon. members may remember having listened to me on a number of occasions referring to the fact that our area was not designated for special assistance. We looked with a jaundiced eye on some of the areas that were so designated, and after much twisting of arms, the area was designated for a short term under the old program. Now, it is designated under the new program.
Northeastern Ontario continues to lose its population. We are not like other parts of Canada which have been doubling their population. Twenty years from now we may be only a recreation area, and people will be going there to hunt and fish in the clear waters because there will be nobody there to dirty them. I think this is really the purpose of the people of that area. We have improved our education, which is a necessity for the development of industry. Someone may ask: "Why would you want computer technicians in northern Ontario?" I am sure I do not know because we do not have any computers, but we are turning out, through a very beautiful college in Kirkland Lake, computer operators who obviously have to go to Toronto to get a job. The same is true of dozens of courses that are being provided for our young people. We are providing the machinery and the facilities that are necessary. We have many advantages but there are many that we still lack.
The previous speaker mentioned our inability in Canada to solve the constitutional problem. Our federal government is so concerned with giving autonomy to the provinces that any program we design federally is watered down by whatever initiative the provincial government takes in this regard. I remember recently a project approved by the federal development agency which had to be withdrawn because the Ontario government had not put in their share. It would seem to me that if we are going to have a program, surely the two governments should get together to make it possible for some type of equal development of the project to take place. But that is not what happens.
Another problem with which we are faced is lack of co-operation with regard to education. The other day I had a visit from some young students from northern Ontario who attend a technical college there. Their complaint was that they could not obtain a student loan, although the federal government provides that kind of money. Why could they not receive this type of grant? Apparently the answer is that they reside in the province of Quebec. They indicated to me that is only one English school in Quebec where they could have obtained this kind of technical education, so they came to Ontario. Until this year, Ontario has provided them with a grant
as if they were residents of Ontario. This year they are about to complete their courses, but now it is said that because these people live in Quebec that province must make the grant. Mr. Speaker, it is the federal govern-1 ment which provides the money. But Ontario says that because they are now going to a designated school in Ontario, even though there is not one in Quebec, they will not be provided with a grant. As a result, they may have to quit at Christmas. They live 50 or 60 miles from this school. The only other similar school is Dawson College in Montreal, about 400 miles away. It is already full and could not accommodate them.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
One of the methods of solving regional disparity must be the provision of better education. The complaint has been made that new industry must be established in the centre of a large educational pool from which it can draw the technical people it needs. Yet in some areas where the educational facilities have been provided, people have received no other advantage than that of being able to send their children to school in that area. Then, they have had to export the finished product, so to speak, to the industrial markets.
Our record is not good. We have had some new industries established in Northern Ontario. I refer in particular to two announced recently by the Department of Regional Expansion in its "Report on the Operation of the Regional Development Incentives Act for the Period September 1 to September 30, 1970" published on October 14. The first is Ecstall Mining Limited, of Toronto, Ontario. Mr. Speaker, in effect, this is Texas Gulf, one of the largest mining companies on the continent. They have located their new plant at Hoyle, just outside Timmins. The type of industry is an electrolytic zinc plant. The bulletin describes the project as a new facility.
Why is it a new facility? It is because the province of Ontario finally made up its mind that if this company was not going to process the product before exporting it, then the government would not allow them to export it. The estimated capital cost is given as $45,700,000, and estimated employment as 360. What did we offer them? We offered them 11 per cent of the approved capital costs and $2,000 per job. The same company is putting up another plant in the same place, Hoyle Township. The type of industry is described in the bulletin as "roasting and sulphuric acid." It is a new facility, and the estimated capital cost is $17,200,000. Estimated employment will be 90 people. We have offered 11 per cent of the approved capital costs and $2,000 per job. If there was ever a company in this country that did not need such assistance it is that company. Mr. Speaker, that company is well able to look after itself.
We gave that company a tax holiday. We gave it other advantages. All the minerals it is going to mine have belonged to Canada. This is an extensive operation, and in return that company will supply us with 360 jobs in one plant, maybe 400 jobs in the mines, and possibly 90 jobs in the sulphuric acid plant. That's a great big deal, Mr. Speaker! That company could not possibly place

November 18, 1970

these facilities anywhere else. Ontario provincial law made it place them there.
I have looked over the projects listed for Quebec, which is fortunate in having the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) as one of its representatives. Exactly the same picture applies there. There are food processing plants. Obviously, you process the food where you produce it. Then, there are saw mills. Obviously, you cut the logs into lumber where you produce them. I am not objecting to Quebec having these plants. If we have the money to supply them, then all well and good. But, Mr. Speaker, one of these days we will have to take a real look at what we want in the way of regional development.
We will have to assess the cost of putting industries in our major cities, new industries which will involve new subways, new highways, new recreational facilities, and more expensive pollution and environmental control. We will have to weigh all these things, and then decide whether there is an advantage in putting new industry in major cities. Every time I travel beyond a major city I go for at least ten miles before reaching the outskirts of it, and that ten miles is taken up with industrial plants. This is true of Quebec City, Hamilton, Toronto, Montreal, Windsor, Vancouver or any other major city you care to name. Yet in my area a number of mines have been closed down, and some 4,000 to 5,000 people are living in communities that could support small factories employing about 100 people.
It is on this point that the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings is right. If a factory is placed in a small community, and we do not charge the company any taxes for a period of ten years, it will at least keep the 100 people it employs off the welfare rolls. In the mining communities we have the highest welfare rate in the province of Ontario, running somewhere from 4 per cent to 6 per cent. Welfare is our biggest industry. If we did
Employment Programs
not have that kind of welfare the communities would be bankrupt.
If we put a factory in such a community we would have 100 people working. They would pay municipal taxes. They would want new sewers, and new water supply. They might require more buildings, and in that way would generate more employment. For every person employed in the factory, probably two or three others would be employed in service industries. Why can't the municipalities do that now? It is because in Ontario there is a law which says that municipalities are not allowed to write off taxes against new industries. That is a mistake and should be corrected.
Until we really decide we want to maintain growth centres in Canada and put new industries in them, until we decide we are really interested in providing reasonable economic expansion, reasonable educational and health facilities, and all the other things that are included in the benefits of industrial development, we will only be giving handouts to companies that are going to settle in certain areas any way. We will make it easier for those companies, but the taxpayers will derive no benefit from the money spent. The net result will be that the dividend collectors will be really well off.
We in Northern Ontario are getting more advantage from the $10 million that is spent on emergency gold mining assistance than we will get out of most of the projects that are connected with regional expansion. That is a wrong way to proceed, Mr. Speaker. It is a disgrace when a subsidy provides employment which cannot be obtained through other methods.
